---
title: "Specification menu"
subtitle: "The fourteen decisions, by group"
bibliography: [references.bib, references-new.bib]
---

Any analysis of the claim has to make a series of decisions, and what follows presents each decision, the options that it offers and whether each option is a justifiable way of answering the claim. In the wording taken by SCORE from the original author's paper [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], the claim is that "poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (p. 619). The workshop interprets it as a claim about change within countries over time, that is, about whether citizens in the member states of 2004–2013 came to frame the EU in less positive terms than before as their national economy deteriorated. The hypothesis from which the claim was taken, and the data on which it rests, are described on the [background page](background.qmd#sec-questions).

Between those data and a verdict on the claim lie fourteen decisions, most of which offer more than one option that a competent analyst might choose. The workshop has examined every option for whether it is a justifiable way of answering this claim and has crossed the justifiable options into the 864 specifications that form the curve of the claim, with the consequence that whatever disagreement remains on the curve is disagreement between defensible analyses. Each option excluded from the curve is presented below with the reason for its exclusion and a link to the module in which it is taught.

The menu is arranged by the three groups into which the decisions fall. Decisions about **the question** change what is being estimated, which means that two people who choose differently are answering different questions and that the results obtained by the two are not rival estimates of one quantity. **Measurement** decisions change how a named quantity is measured, leaving the question as it is. Decisions about **the model** change neither the question nor the measures, but only how the model is fitted and how uncertain its answer is said to be.

## The decision map {#map}

```{r}
#| include: false
# Data for the decision map, read once at render: every option of the full menu,
# the curve of the claim, the curve of the negative scales, every option set
# against its twins on the curve, and the titles of the pages that teach each
# option. All of it is aggregate. The pairs travel as three short arrays per
# option and test (twin on the curve, r of the alternative, p < 0.05 or not),
# which keeps the page small. The inference rules need no pairs, because the
# curve file carries every p-value.

axes <- c("outcome", "predictor", "copredictor", "estimator", "sample", "weights",
          "construction", "noop", "item_set", "cell_weight", "measure", "pred_form", "family")
vary <- c("outcome", "predictor", "copredictor", "estimator", "noop", "item_set",
          "cell_weight", "measure", "pred_form")

menu <- readr::read_csv("data/menu_options.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("r_ca") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(idx = seq_along(r_ca) - 1L)
curve_neg <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve_negative.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
deviations <- readr::read_csv("data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
twin_index <- datawizard::data_select(curve, select = c(axes, "idx"))
pair_rows <- readr::read_csv("data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive" & axis != "se") |>
  dplyr::left_join(twin_index, by = axes)
stopifnot(!anyNA(pair_rows$idx), nrow(curve) == 864)

pairs <- pair_rows |>
  datawizard::data_modify(key = paste(axis, option, rule, sep = "|")) |>
  split(~key) |>
  purrr::map(\(d) list(i = d$idx, r = round(d$r_ca_dev, 4), s = as.integer(d$p_dev < 0.05)))

# the cells and countries left by the two series that do not cover the panel
coverage <- pair_rows |>
  datawizard::data_filter(option %in% c("es_1574_tips", "es_growth")) |>
  dplyr::distinct(option, n_cells_dev, n_countries_dev) |>
  split(~option) |>
  purrr::map(\(d) list(cells = d$n_cells_dev[1], countries = d$n_countries_dev[1]))

curve_js <- curve |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(vary)), idx,
    r_ca = round(r_ca, 4),
    p_conv = signif(p_conv, 3), p_cr1 = signif(p_cr1, 3), p_cr2 = signif(p_cr2, 3),
    ref = is_reference
  )
neg_js <- curve_neg |>
  dplyr::transmute(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(vary)), r_ca = round(r_ca, 4),
                   p_cr2 = signif(p_cr2, 3))

# page titles without their Markdown emphasis, for the links to the teaching pages;
# a path that ends in the id of a section takes the title of its page
pages <- unique(menu$taught_on) |>
  purrr::set_names() |>
  purrr::map(\(f) gsub("*", "", rmarkdown::yaml_front_matter(sub("#.*", "", f))$title, fixed = TRUE))

ojs_define(menu_raw = menu, curve_raw = curve_js, neg_raw = neg_js, dev_raw = deviations,
           pairs_raw = pairs, coverage_raw = coverage, pages_raw = pages)
```

Every decision that an analysis of the claim has to make appears on the map in the order in which an analyst encounters it on the way from the data to a verdict. The map opens on the workshop's reproduced specification and displays for each decision all of its options, both those on the curve of 864 specifications and those that are taught in the workshop but have been removed from the curve. The options removed from the curve are those that answer another question or answer this one less well.

Selecting an option rewrites the estimand statement, marking the phrases changed by the choice, and opens a description stating what the option estimates and whether it is a justifiable way of answering the claim. The description also reports how the results change when the option is swapped into the specifications of the curve, and names the place in the workshop where it is taught. The full reasoning behind each option, and the evidence on which it rests, are presented in the sections below the map.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// Data and constants of the map. This chunk displays nothing: a named cell
// whose value is not a DOM node would otherwise print as an inspector line.
menu = transpose(menu_raw)
curve = transpose(curve_raw)
negCurve = transpose(neg_raw)
devRows = transpose(dev_raw)
VARY = ["outcome", "predictor", "copredictor", "estimator", "noop", "item_set", "cell_weight", "measure", "pred_form"]
ALL_AXES = ["sample", "outcome", "construction", "noop", "item_set", "cell_weight", "predictor", "measure", "pred_form", "estimator", "copredictor", "weights", "family", "se"]
curveKey = d => VARY.map(a => d[a]).join("|")
curveIndex = new Map(curve.map((d, k) => [curveKey(d), k]))
negIndex = new Map(negCurve.map((d, k) => [curveKey(d), k]))

DM = {
  return {
    stages: [
      {id: "data", title: "The data and the sample", note: "Which country-years enter the analysis, and so which population the answer describes.", axes: ["sample"]},
      {id: "outcome", title: "The outcome", note: "How the answers to the question on what the EU means become one number for each country-year.", axes: ["outcome", "construction", "noop", "item_set", "cell_weight"]},
      {id: "predictor", title: "The predictor", note: "Which figure stands for poor national economic performance, and in what form it enters.", axes: ["predictor", "measure", "pred_form"]},
      {id: "comparison", title: "The comparison", note: "Which country-years are compared with which, and what is held fixed while they are compared.", axes: ["estimator", "copredictor"]},
      {id: "average", title: "Whose average", note: "How much each country-year counts in the slope.", axes: ["weights"]},
      {id: "model", title: "The model form", note: "The model that is fitted to the cell means.", axes: ["family"]},
      {id: "inference", title: "The inference", note: "How uncertain the slope is said to be, which decides its class on the curve.", axes: ["se"]}
    ],
    colour: {outcome: "#0e3b6a", construction: "#1f4c7c", predictor: "#2a5d8f", copredictor: "#4a78ab", sample: "#0f6b6b", weights: "#2b8585", estimator: "#8c5a10",
             noop: "#4a7a3f", item_set: "#4a7a3f", cell_weight: "#4a7a3f", measure: "#4a7a3f", pred_form: "#7b6a8f", family: "#7b6a8f", se: "#7b6a8f"},
    levelName: {estimand: "The question", measurement: "Measurement", estimation: "The model"},
    levelShort: {estimand: "Question", measurement: "Measurement", estimation: "Model"},
    judgement: {kept: "On the curve", other_question: "Another question", weaker_answer: "A weaker answer", check: "A check"},
    ruleLabel: {cr2: "CR2 errors with Satterthwaite df", re_conventional: "model-based errors", re_cr1_g1: "errors clustered by country (CR1, 26 df)",
                rewb_satterthwaite: "Satterthwaite df", rewb_cr2: "CR2 errors with Satterthwaite df", beta_cr1_g1: "errors clustered by country (CR1, 26 df)",
                mi_rubin_cr1_g1: "a clustered test pooled over ten imputations (26 df)", conventional: "conventional errors", cr1_g1: "errors clustered by country (CR1, 26 df)",
                identical_to_count: "the test of the count"},
    preferredRule: {re: "re_cr1_g1", rewb: "rewb_cr2", beta: "beta_cr1_g1", mi_mice: "mi_rubin_cr1_g1", mi_amelia: "mi_rubin_cr1_g1"},
    sePcol: {cr2: "p_cr2", cr1: "p_cr1", conventional: "p_conv"},
    seDev: {cr1: "cr1_g1", conventional: "conventional"},
    seName: {cr2: "CR2 errors", cr1: "CR1 errors", conventional: "conventional errors"},
    kItems: {all: {mcosmo: 5, mutil: 2, mcomm: 4, mlib: 2, mpos: 7, mneg: 6}, un: {mcosmo: 5, mutil: 2, mcomm: 3, mlib: 2, mpos: 7, mneg: 5}},
    numWord: {2: "two", 3: "three", 4: "four", 5: "five", 6: "six", 7: "seven"},
    negativeOutcomes: ["mcomm", "mlib", "mneg"],
    domainR: [-0.66, 0.32]
  };
}

// numbers as the site prints them: fixed decimals and a true minus sign
fmtR = x => (x < 0 ? "−" : "") + Math.abs(x).toFixed(3)
// four decimals below 0.001 and within 0.005 of the threshold, so that a p
// just above 0.05 never prints as 0.050
fmtP = p => p < 0.0001 ? "< 0.0001" : p < 0.001 || Math.abs(p - 0.05) < 0.005 ? p.toFixed(4) : p.toFixed(3)
// "p = 0.029" or "p < 0.0001", so that a bound never follows an equals sign
pEq = p => p < 0.0001 ? "p < 0.0001" : `p = ${fmtP(p)}`
fmtPct = x => x.toFixed(1) + "%"
```

::: {.column-page}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
decisionMap = {
  const opt = (axis, code) => menu.find(d => d.axis === axis && d.option === code);
  const optionsOf = axis => menu.filter(d => d.axis === axis);
  const col = axis => DM.colour[axis];
  const el = (tag, attrs, ...kids) => {
    const n = document.createElement(tag);
    if (attrs) for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(attrs)) {
      if (k === "class") n.className = v;
      else if (k === "text") n.textContent = v;
      else if (k === "style") n.setAttribute("style", v);
      else n.setAttribute(k, v);
    }
    for (const kid of kids) if (kid !== null && kid !== undefined) n.append(kid);
    return n;
  };
  // the first ".qmd" of a path, so that the id of a section after it stays in the address
  const pageLink = file => el("a", {href: file.replace(".qmd", ".html")}, pages_raw[file] || file);

  // ---- state: one option per decision, starting from the reproduced specification
  const refRow = curve.find(d => d.ref === true);
  const REF = {sample: "all", weights: "none", construction: "share", family: "gaussian", se: "cr2"};
  for (const a of VARY) REF[a] = refRow[a];
  let sel = Object.assign({}, REF);
  let lastOn = Object.assign({}, REF);
  let lastUnempSeries = REF.measure;
  let latest = null;
  let prevText = null;

  const isOn = (s, a) => opt(a, s[a]).on_curve === true;
  const offAxes = s => ALL_AXES.filter(a => !isOn(s, a));

  // the specification on the curve that stands in for every off-curve choice
  // with the last on-curve option of that decision
  function twinOf(s) {
    const t = Object.assign({}, s);
    for (const a of ALL_AXES) if (!isOn(s, a)) t[a] = lastOn[a];
    if (t.predictor === "growth") { t.measure = "wb_growth"; t.pred_form = "raw"; }
    else if (t.measure === "wb_growth" || t.measure === "es_growth") t.measure = lastUnempSeries;
    return t;
  }
  const curveRowOf = s => { const k = curveIndex.get(curveKey(s)); return k === undefined ? null : curve[k]; };

  function choose(axis, code) {
    const prev = Object.assign({}, sel);
    sel[axis] = code;
    if (axis === "predictor") {
      if (code === "growth") { sel.measure = prev.measure === "es_growth" ? "es_growth" : "wb_growth"; sel.pred_form = "raw"; }
      else if (sel.measure === "wb_growth" || sel.measure === "es_growth") sel.measure = lastUnempSeries;
    }
    if (axis === "measure") {
      const growthSeries = code === "wb_growth" || code === "es_growth";
      sel.predictor = growthSeries ? "growth" : "unemp";
      if (growthSeries) sel.pred_form = "raw";
    }
    for (const a of ALL_AXES) if (isOn(sel, a)) lastOn[a] = sel[a];
    if (sel.predictor === "unemp" && isOn(sel, "measure")) lastUnempSeries = sel.measure;
    latest = axis;
  }

  // ---- the estimand statement, as segments that can be compared with the last one
  function statement(s) {
    const o = a => opt(a, s[a]);
    const k = DM.kItems[s.item_set][s.outcome];
    const outcomeText = o("construction").phrase.replace("{frames}", o("outcome").phrase).replace("{k}", DM.numWord[k]);
    let sampleText = o("sample").phrase;
    if (s.measure === "es_1574_tips") {
      const c = coverage_raw.es_1574_tips;
      sampleText = s.sample === "all"
        ? `the ${c.cells} country-years that the Eurostat table tipsun20 covers, from ${c.countries} member states without the United Kingdom and, before 2009, only France and Sweden`
        : `${sampleText}, and of these only the country-years that the Eurostat table tipsun20 covers`;
    }
    if (s.measure === "es_growth") {
      const c = coverage_raw.es_growth;
      sampleText = s.sample === "all"
        ? `the ${c.cells} country-years of the ${c.countries} member states other than the United Kingdom, which the Eurostat growth series does not cover`
        : `${sampleText}, without the United Kingdom`;
    }
    const other = s.predictor === "unemp" ? "GDP growth" : "the unemployment rate";
    const predName = s.predictor === "unemp" ? "unemployment" : "GDP growth";
    const seg = (key, text, lv, colourAxis) => ({key, text, lv, colourAxis: colourAxis || key});
    return {
      question: [
        "Among ", seg("sample", sampleText, "l1"), ", with ", seg("weights", o("weights").phrase, "l1"),
        ", the association between ", seg("predictor", o("predictor").phrase, "l1"),
        " (", seg("measure", o("measure").phrase, "l2"), ") and ", seg("outcome", outcomeText, "l1"),
        " (", seg("item_set", o("item_set").phrase, "l2"), ", ", seg("noop", o("noop").phrase, "l2"), ", ",
        seg("cell_weight", o("cell_weight").phrase, "l2"), "), comparing ", seg("estimator", o("estimator").phrase, "l1"),
        ", ", seg("copredictor", o("copredictor").phrase.replace("{other}", other), "l1"), "."
      ],
      method: [
        "Answered with ", seg("family", o("family").phrase, "l3"), ", ",
        seg("pred_form", o("pred_form").phrase.replace("{pred}", predName), "l3"), ", and tested by ", seg("se", o("se").phrase, "l3"), "."
      ]
    };
  }
  function renderSegments(target, parts) {
    target.replaceChildren();
    for (const p of parts) {
      if (typeof p === "string") { target.append(p); continue; }
      const span = el("span", {class: `dm-seg ${p.lv}`, style: `--c:${col(p.colourAxis)}`, text: p.text});
      const changed = prevText !== null && prevText[p.key] !== undefined && prevText[p.key] !== p.text;
      target.append(changed ? el("mark", {class: "dm-changed"}, span) : span);
    }
  }

  // ---- what the selection gives
  function pairKey(axis, code) {
    const c = axis === "construction" && code === "rate" ? "count" : code;
    const rule = DM.preferredRule[c] || "cr2";
    const key = `${axis}|${c}|${rule}`;
    return pairs_raw[key] ? {key, rule} : null;
  }
  function verdictOf(s) {
    if (s.family === "beta" && s.construction === "count") return {kind: "inadmissible"};
    const off = offAxes(s).filter(a => a !== "se");
    if (off.length === 0) {
      const d = curveRowOf(s);
      const p = d[DM.sePcol[s.se]];
      return {kind: "curve", d, p, rule: s.se};
    }
    if (off.length === 1 && off[0] === "outcome" && DM.negativeOutcomes.includes(s.outcome)) {
      const k = negIndex.get(curveKey(s));
      return {kind: "negative", d: k === undefined ? null : negCurve[k]};
    }
    if (off.length === 1) {
      const a = off[0], pk = pairKey(a, s[a]);
      const twin = curveRowOf(twinOf(s));
      if (pk === null || twin === null) return {kind: "unfitted", axes: off};
      const P = pairs_raw[pk.key];
      const k = P.i.indexOf(twin.idx);
      if (k < 0) return {kind: "outside", axis: a, twin};
      return {kind: "refit", axis: a, rule: pk.rule, r: P.r[k], sig: P.s[k] === 1, twin};
    }
    return {kind: "unfitted", axes: off};
  }

  // ---- the map
  const stageEls = {};
  const chipEls = [];
  const verdictBox = el("p", {class: "dm-verdict", "aria-live": "polite"});
  const resetBtn = el("button", {type: "button", class: "dm-reset"}, "Back to the reproduced specification");
  const stagesBox = el("div", {class: "dm-stages"});
  DM.stages.forEach((st, si) => {
    const box = el("section", {class: "dm-stage", "aria-labelledby": `dm-stage-${st.id}`},
      el("div", {class: "dm-stage-head"}, el("span", {class: "dm-stage-num", "aria-hidden": "true"}, String(si + 1)),
        el("h3", {id: `dm-stage-${st.id}`}, st.title)),
      el("p", {class: "dm-stage-note"}, st.note));
    for (const axis of st.axes) {
      const opts = optionsOf(axis);
      const first = opts[0];
      const nameId = `dm-dec-${axis}`;
      const group = el("div", {class: "dm-chips", role: "group", "aria-labelledby": nameId});
      for (const o of opts) {
        const tip = o.on_curve ? `${o.label}: on the curve` : `${o.label}: off the curve, taught on ${pages_raw[o.taught_on] || o.taught_on}`;
        const b = el("button", {type: "button", class: "dm-chip" + (o.on_curve ? "" : " off"), style: `--c:${col(axis)}`,
                                "aria-pressed": "false", title: tip, "aria-label": tip, "data-tip": tip}, o.label);
        b.addEventListener("click", () => {
          if (b.getAttribute("aria-disabled") === "true") return;
          const before = b.getBoundingClientRect().top;
          choose(axis, o.option);
          update(st.id);
          const after = b.getBoundingClientRect().top;
          if (Math.abs(after - before) > 1) window.scrollBy(0, after - before);
        });
        chipEls.push({b, axis, code: o.option});
        group.append(b);
      }
      box.append(el("div", {class: "dm-decision"},
        el("div", {class: "dm-decision-name", id: nameId}, first.decision,
          el("span", {class: "lv", style: `color:${col(axis)}`}, DM.levelShort[first.level])),
        group));
    }
    stageEls[st.id] = box;
    stagesBox.append(box);
  });
  const verdictStage = el("section", {class: "dm-stage", "aria-labelledby": "dm-stage-verdict"},
    el("div", {class: "dm-stage-head"}, el("span", {class: "dm-stage-num", "aria-hidden": "true"}, String(DM.stages.length + 1)),
      el("h3", {id: "dm-stage-verdict"}, "The verdict")),
    verdictBox, resetBtn);
  stagesBox.append(verdictStage);
  resetBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const before = resetBtn.getBoundingClientRect().top;
    sel = Object.assign({}, REF); lastOn = Object.assign({}, REF); lastUnempSeries = REF.measure;
    latest = null; update(null);
    const after = resetBtn.getBoundingClientRect().top;
    if (Math.abs(after - before) > 1) window.scrollBy(0, after - before);
  });

  // ---- the panel: statement, the selected option, its twins, the curve
  const statementP = el("p", {class: "dm-statement", "aria-live": "polite"});
  const methodP = el("p", {class: "dm-method"});
  const changedNote = el("p", {class: "dm-small"});
  const optionBox = el("div");
  const pairBox = el("div");
  const curveBox = el("div");
  const panel = el("div", {class: "dm-panel", role: "region", "aria-label": "The selection and its results"},
    el("h3", {}, "The estimand statement"), statementP, methodP, changedNote,
    el("h3", {}, "The selected option"), optionBox,
    el("h3", {}, "Against its twins on the curve"), pairBox,
    el("h3", {}, "The curve of 864"), curveBox);
  const side = el("div", {class: "dm-side"});
  const topSlot = el("div");
  const layout = el("div", {class: "dm-layout"}, el("div", {}, topSlot, stagesBox), side);

  const legend = el("div", {class: "dm-legend"},
    el("span", {}, el("span", {class: "sw", style: "background:#0e3b6a"}), el("span", {class: "sw", style: "background:#0f6b6b"}), el("span", {class: "sw", style: "background:#8c5a10"}), DM.levelName.estimand),
    el("span", {}, el("span", {class: "sw", style: "background:#4a7a3f"}), DM.levelName.measurement),
    el("span", {}, el("span", {class: "sw", style: "background:#7b6a8f"}), DM.levelName.estimation),
    el("span", {}, el("span", {class: "chip-sample"}, "solid"), "on the curve"),
    el("span", {}, el("span", {class: "chip-sample off"}, "dashed"), "in the workshop, off the curve"));

  const wide = window.matchMedia("(min-width: 1100px)");
  function place(stageId) {
    if (wide.matches) { if (panel.parentNode !== side) side.append(panel); return; }
    if (stageId === null || stageId === undefined) { if (panel.parentNode !== topSlot) topSlot.append(panel); return; }
    const anchor = stageId === "verdict" ? verdictStage : stageEls[stageId];
    if (anchor.nextSibling !== panel) anchor.after(panel);
  }

  // ---- charts
  const recipe = d => VARY.map(a => opt(a, d[a]).label).join("; ");
  function curveChart(width, v) {
    const onAxes = VARY.filter(a => isOn(sel, a));
    const match = curve.filter(d => onAxes.every(a => d[a] === sel[a]));
    const matchSet = new Set(match.map(d => d.idx));
    const showLatest = latest !== null && VARY.includes(latest) && isOn(sel, latest);
    const latestRows = showLatest ? curve.filter(d => d[latest] === sel[latest] && !matchSet.has(d.idx)) : [];
    const latestSet = new Set(latestRows.map(d => d.idx));
    const base = curve.filter(d => !matchSet.has(d.idx) && !latestSet.has(d.idx));
    const x = d => d.idx + 1;
    const dots = (data, stroke, opSig, opNs, r, sw) => [
      Plot.dot(data.filter(d => d.p_cr2 < 0.05), {x, y: "r_ca", r, symbol: "circle", fill: "none", stroke, strokeOpacity: opSig, strokeWidth: sw, title: d => `${recipe(d)}\nr = ${fmtR(d.r_ca)}, CR2 ${pEq(d.p_cr2)}`}),
      Plot.dot(data.filter(d => d.p_cr2 >= 0.05), {x, y: "r_ca", r, symbol: "times", fill: "none", stroke, strokeOpacity: opNs, strokeWidth: sw, title: d => `${recipe(d)}\nr = ${fmtR(d.r_ca)}, CR2 ${pEq(d.p_cr2)}`})
    ];
    const ref = curve.filter(d => d.ref === true);
    const marks = [
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#9aa8b3", strokeWidth: 0.8}),
      ...dots(base, "#1d2731", 0.25, 0.12, 3.6, 0.7),
      ...dots(latestRows, col(latest || "outcome"), 0.65, 0.5, 3.6, 0.9),
      ...dots(match, "#8b1538", 1, 1, 5.5, 1.6),
      Plot.text(ref, {x, y: "r_ca", text: () => "reproduced", dy: 16, fontSize: 10, fill: "#1d2731"})
    ];
    if (v.kind === "refit") {
      marks.push(Plot.ruleY([v.r], {stroke: "#8b1538", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeWidth: 1}));
      marks.push(Plot.text([v.r], {x: 860, y: d => d, text: () => `refitted: r = ${fmtR(v.r)}`, textAnchor: "end", dy: -6, fontSize: 10, fill: "#8b1538"}));
    }
    return Plot.plot({
      width, height: Math.max(230, Math.min(320, Math.round(width * 0.5))), marginLeft: 46, marginRight: 10, marginBottom: 38,
      style: {fontSize: "11px", background: "transparent"},
      ariaLabel: "The curve of 864 specifications, with the current selection marked",
      x: {domain: [0, 865], label: "864 specifications, ranked by claim-aligned r →", ticks: 4},
      y: {domain: DM.domainR, label: "↑ Claim-aligned partial r", grid: true, ticks: 5},
      marks
    });
  }
  function pairData(axis, code) {
    if (axis === "se") {
      const yCol = DM.sePcol[code];
      const xCol = code === "cr2" ? "p_conv" : "p_cr2";
      return curve.map(d => {
        const xv = Math.max(d[xCol], 1e-4), yv = Math.max(d[yCol], 1e-4);
        const cx = d.r_ca < 0 && d[xCol] < 0.05, cy = d.r_ca < 0 && d[yCol] < 0.05;
        return {x: xv, y: yv, s: d[yCol] < 0.05, changed: cx !== cy, twin: d, label: recipe(d)};
      });
    }
    const pk = pairKey(axis, code);
    if (pk === null) return null;
    const P = pairs_raw[pk.key];
    return P.i.map((ti, k) => {
      const t = curve[ti];
      const twinClass = t.r_ca < 0 && t.p_cr2 < 0.05, devClass = P.r[k] < 0 && P.s[k] === 1;
      return {x: t.r_ca, y: P.r[k], s: P.s[k] === 1, changed: twinClass !== devClass, twin: t, label: recipe(t)};
    });
  }
  function pairChart(width, axis, code, data, isSelPair) {
    const isSe = axis === "se";
    const same = data.filter(d => !d.changed), moved = data.filter(d => d.changed);
    const selPair = data.filter(d => isSelPair(d.twin));
    const c = col(axis);
    const dots = (rows, stroke, op, r, sw) => [
      Plot.dot(rows.filter(d => d.s), {x: "x", y: "y", r, symbol: "circle", fill: "none", stroke, strokeOpacity: op, strokeWidth: sw, title: d => `${d.label}\n${fmtR(d.x)} → ${fmtR(d.y)}`}),
      Plot.dot(rows.filter(d => !d.s), {x: "x", y: "y", r, symbol: "times", fill: "none", stroke, strokeOpacity: op * 0.8, strokeWidth: sw, title: d => `${d.label}\n${fmtR(d.x)} → ${fmtR(d.y)}`})
    ];
    const lo = isSe ? 1e-4 : DM.domainR[0], hi = isSe ? 1 : DM.domainR[1];
    const xName = isSe ? (code === "cr2" ? "p under conventional errors" : "p under CR2, the rule of the curve") : "claim-aligned r on the curve";
    const yName = isSe ? `p under ${DM.seName[code]}` : "claim-aligned r with this option";
    return Plot.plot({
      width, height: Math.max(240, Math.min(360, Math.round(width * 0.62))), marginLeft: 50, marginRight: 12, marginBottom: 40,
      style: {fontSize: "11px", background: "transparent"},
      ariaLabel: `Each specification on the curve set against the same specification with ${opt(axis, code).label}`,
      x: isSe ? {type: "log", domain: [lo, hi], label: `${xName} →`, ticks: 4, tickFormat: "~g"} : {domain: [lo, hi], label: `${xName} →`, ticks: 5},
      y: isSe ? {type: "log", domain: [lo, hi], label: `↑ ${yName}`, ticks: 4, tickFormat: "~g"} : {domain: [lo, hi], label: `↑ ${yName}`, ticks: 5},
      marks: [
        isSe ? Plot.ruleX([0.05], {stroke: "#9aa8b3", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}) : Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#9aa8b3", strokeWidth: 0.8}),
        isSe ? Plot.ruleY([0.05], {stroke: "#9aa8b3", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}) : Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#9aa8b3", strokeWidth: 0.8}),
        Plot.line([[lo, lo], [hi, hi]], {stroke: "#5b6b78", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeWidth: 0.8}),
        ...dots(same, "#1d2731", 0.3, 3.4, 0.7),
        ...dots(moved, c, 0.75, 3.4, 0.9),
        ...dots(selPair, "#8b1538", 1, 6, 1.8)
      ]
    });
  }

  // ---- the selected option, in words and numbers
  const curveShares = {
    below: 100 * d3.mean(curve, d => d.r_ca < 0 ? 1 : 0),
    sig: 100 * d3.mean(curve, d => d.r_ca < 0 && d.p_cr2 < 0.05 ? 1 : 0)
  };
  function summaryText(axis, code, o) {
    const negative = axis === "outcome" && DM.negativeOutcomes.includes(code);
    const devCode = axis === "se" ? DM.seDev[code] : code;
    const rows = devRows.filter(d => d.curve === (negative ? "negative" : "positive") && d.axis === axis && d.option === devCode);
    const out = [];
    if (negative) {
      const r = rows[0];
      out.push(el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, `The curve of this claim holds no specification of this scale. On the curve of the negative scales, aligned so that below zero is the direction of the other half of the hypothesis, its 288 specifications lie below zero in ${fmtPct(r.below_zero)} of cases and below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 in ${fmtPct(r.below_zero_sig)}, with a median claim-aligned r of ${fmtR(r.median_r_ca)}.`));
      return out;
    }
    if (axis === "se" && code === "cr2") {
      const conv = 100 * d3.mean(curve, d => d.r_ca < 0 && d.p_conv < 0.05 ? 1 : 0);
      out.push(el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, `Every point of the curve is classed by this rule: ${fmtPct(curveShares.sig)} of the 864 specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against ${fmtPct(conv)} under conventional errors. The partial correlation is the same under every rule, so only the class moves.`));
      return out;
    }
    const withPairs = rows.filter(r => r.n_pairs > 0);
    if (withPairs.length === 0) {
      out.push(el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, code === "wb_growth"
        ? "This is the only growth series on the curve, so there is no other series on the curve to set it against; the Eurostat growth series is compared with it."
        : `Every specification on the curve uses this option, so there is nothing on the curve to set it against; the alternatives on the map are compared with it. On the curve itself ${fmtPct(curveShares.below)} of the 864 specifications lie below zero and ${fmtPct(curveShares.sig)} below zero with CR2 p < 0.05.`));
      return out;
    }
    for (const r of withPairs) {
      const rule = DM.ruleLabel[r.rule] || r.rule;
      const lead = o.on_curve
        ? `Among the ${r.n_pairs} pairs of specifications on the curve that differ only in this decision, the specifications with this option lie below zero in ${fmtPct(r.below_zero)} of cases and below zero with p < 0.05 under ${rule} in ${fmtPct(r.below_zero_sig)}.`
        : `Swapped into the ${r.n_pairs} specifications of the curve to which it applies, this option leaves ${fmtPct(r.below_zero)} of them below zero and ${fmtPct(r.below_zero_sig)} below zero with p < 0.05 under ${rule}, against ${fmtPct(curveShares.sig)} on the curve itself.`;
      const rest = axis === "se"
        ? ` The partial correlations stay as they are, so only the class can move, and it moves for ${fmtPct(r.class_changes)} of the specifications.`
        : ` Their median claim-aligned r is ${fmtR(r.median_r_ca)}, a median shift of ${fmtR(r.median_shift)} from their twins; ${fmtPct(r.sign_changes)} of the pairs change sign and ${fmtPct(r.class_changes)} change class.`;
      out.push(el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, lead + rest));
    }
    if (withPairs.some(r => r.rule !== "cr2" && axis !== "se"))
      out.push(el("p", {class: "dm-small"}, "Part of the change of class comes from the test, because this option is tested by a different rule from the CR2 rule of the curve."));
    return out;
  }

  function renderOption(width, v, twinSel) {
    optionBox.replaceChildren();
    pairBox.replaceChildren();
    if (latest === null) {
      optionBox.append(el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, "The map opens on the reproduced specification: the cosmopolitan share on World Bank unemployment, compared within countries net of the common yearly changes, with respondents who mention nothing scored zero, all 13 items and cells as interviewed. Select any option on the map to read what it estimates and whether it answers the claim."));
      pairBox.append(el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, "Once an option is selected, a chart here sets each specification on the curve against the same specification with that option."));
      return;
    }
    const axis = latest, code = sel[axis], o = opt(axis, code), c = col(axis);
    optionBox.append(
      el("p", {class: "dm-option-title"}, `${o.decision}: ${o.label}`),
      el("span", {class: "dm-badge", style: `--c:${c}`}, DM.levelName[o.level]),
      el("span", {class: "dm-badge" + (o.on_curve ? "" : " off"), style: `--c:${o.on_curve ? "#1d2731" : "#8b1538"}`}, DM.judgement[o.judgement]),
      el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, el("b", {}, "What it estimates. "), o.estimates),
      el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, el("b", {}, o.on_curve ? "Why it is on the curve. " : "Why it is off the curve. "), o.explanation),
      el("p", {class: "dm-small"}, "Taught on ", pageLink(o.taught_on), "."));
    for (const p of summaryText(axis, code, o)) pairBox.append(p);
    const data = DM.negativeOutcomes.includes(code) && axis === "outcome" ? null : pairData(axis, code);
    if (data !== null && data.length > 0) {
      const box = el("div", {class: "dm-chart"});
      // the pairs of the selection: twins that match it on every decision but this
      // one (the series and form follow a change of predictor)
      const free = a => a === axis || (axis === "predictor" && (a === "measure" || a === "pred_form"));
      const isSelPair = t => twinSel !== null && VARY.every(a => free(a) || t[a] === twinSel[a]);
      box.append(pairChart(width, axis, code, data, isSelPair));
      pairBox.append(box);
      const label = o.label;
      const caption = axis === "se"
        ? `Each mark is one of the 864 specifications on the curve, placed by its p-value under ${code === "cr2" ? "conventional errors" : "CR2, the rule of the curve"} (horizontal) and under ${DM.seName[code]} (vertical), on logarithmic scales; values below 0.0001 are drawn at 0.0001. The dashed lines mark p = 0.05 and the diagonal marks equal p-values. Circles are significant at 5% on the vertical rule, crosses are not; coloured marks change class (below zero with p < 0.05, or not) between the two rules. The burgundy mark is the specification of the current selection.`
        : `Each mark is one pair: a specification on the curve, placed horizontally by its claim-aligned partial r, and the same specification with ${label}, placed vertically. Marks on the dashed diagonal are unchanged, and marks below it lie further in the direction of the claim. Circles are significant at 5% under the test of the option, crosses are not; coloured marks change class (below zero with p < 0.05, or not) between the two members of the pair. The burgundy mark is the pair of the current selection, where there is one.`;
      pairBox.append(el("p", {class: "dm-caption"}, caption));
    }
  }

  function renderVerdict(v) {
    const parts = [];
    const sym = sig => sig ? "an open circle, significant at 5%" : "a cross, not significant at 5%";
    if (v.kind === "curve") {
      const d = v.d, k = d.idx;
      const ruleTxt = v.rule === "cr2" ? "CR2" : DM.seName[v.rule];
      parts.push(`The selection is one of the 864 specifications on the curve: claim-aligned r = ${fmtR(d.r_ca)}, ${ruleTxt} ${pEq(v.p)}.`);
      if (v.rule !== "cr2") parts.push(` The curve classes it by CR2, ${pEq(d.p_cr2)}, which draws it as ${sym(d.p_cr2 < 0.05)}.`);
      else parts.push(` On the curve it is ${sym(d.p_cr2 < 0.05)}.`);
      parts.push(` On the curve, ${fmtPct(100 * k / 864)} of the specifications lie further in the direction of the claim.`);
      if (sel.predictor === "growth") parts.push(" The sign of growth is reversed on the curve, because the claim expects framing to rise with growth.");
      return parts.join("");
    }
    const off = offAxes(sel).filter(a => a !== "se");
    const why = off.map(a => `${opt(a, sel[a]).decision.toLowerCase()} – ${opt(a, sel[a]).label} (${DM.judgement[opt(a, sel[a]).judgement].toLowerCase()})`).join("; ");
    if (v.kind === "inadmissible") return "A count is a number of items, not a proportion, so the beta family cannot model it, and the menu holds no such analysis.";
    let txt = `The curve holds no analysis with this selection, because of ${off.length === 1 ? "one choice" : "these choices"}: ${why}. The burgundy marks are the specifications on the curve that share every other choice.`;
    if (v.kind === "negative" && v.d) txt += ` On the curve of the negative scales this specification has claim-aligned r = ${fmtR(v.d.r_ca)} and CR2 ${pEq(v.d.p_cr2)}, aligned so that below zero is the direction of the other half of the hypothesis.`;
    if (v.kind === "refit") txt += ` Refitted with this option, the closest specification on the curve moves from r = ${fmtR(v.twin.r_ca)} to r = ${fmtR(v.r)}, ${v.sig ? "with p < 0.05" : "with p ≥ 0.05"} under ${DM.ruleLabel[v.rule]}; the dashed line marks where that refit would sit.`;
    if (v.kind === "outside") txt += " This option was fitted only at the standard measurement settings (raw unemployment in the World Bank series, all items, cells as interviewed), and the selection differs from them, so no refit of it exists.";
    if (v.kind === "unfitted" && off.length > 1) txt += " Each option off the curve was fitted one at a time against the curve, so this combination of options was never fitted.";
    return txt;
  }

  let lastWidth = 0;
  function drawPanel() {
    const width = Math.max(280, Math.floor(panel.clientWidth - 34));
    lastWidth = width;
    const v = verdictOf(sel);
    const twin = curveRowOf(offAxes(sel).filter(a => a !== "se").length === 0 ? sel : twinOf(sel));
    renderOption(width, v, twin);
    curveBox.replaceChildren();
    const box = el("div", {class: "dm-chart"});
    box.append(curveChart(width, v));
    curveBox.append(el("p", {class: "dm-text"}, renderVerdict(v)), box,
      el("p", {class: "dm-caption"}, `Each mark is one of the 864 specifications on the curve of the claim, ranked by its claim-aligned partial r, where below zero is the direction of the claim. Open circles are significant at 5% under CR2 errors clustered by country, crosses are not. Burgundy marks are the specifications that match every on-curve choice of the selection${latest !== null && VARY.includes(latest) && isOn(sel, latest) ? `, and the coloured marks are the other specifications that share the option selected last (${opt(latest, sel[latest]).label})` : ""}. The ink label marks the reproduced specification.`));
  }

  function update(stageId) {
    for (const {b, axis, code} of chipEls) {
      b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", sel[axis] === code ? "true" : "false");
      const disabled = axis === "pred_form" && code === "log" && sel.predictor === "growth";
      b.setAttribute("aria-disabled", disabled ? "true" : "false");
      const tip = disabled ? "Logged: growth takes negative values, so it enters raw only" : b.getAttribute("data-tip");
      b.title = tip;
      b.setAttribute("aria-label", tip);
    }
    const st = statement(sel);
    renderSegments(statementP, st.question);
    renderSegments(methodP, st.method);
    const nowText = {};
    for (const p of [...st.question, ...st.method]) if (typeof p !== "string") nowText[p.key] = p.text;
    const anyChanged = prevText !== null && Object.keys(nowText).some(k => prevText[k] !== nowText[k]);
    changedNote.textContent = anyChanged
      ? "The marked phrases are the ones that the latest choice changed. Bold phrases state the question, green phrases say how its variables are measured, and the second sentence says how the answer is reached."
      : "Bold phrases state the question, green phrases say how its variables are measured, and the second sentence says how the answer is reached.";
    prevText = nowText;
    const v = verdictOf(sel);
    verdictBox.textContent = v.kind === "curve"
      ? `On the curve: r = ${fmtR(v.d.r_ca)}, ${v.rule === "cr2" ? "CR2" : DM.seName[v.rule]} ${pEq(v.p)}${v.rule === "cr2" ? "" : ` (CR2 ${pEq(v.d.p_cr2)})`}.`
      : v.kind === "refit" ? `Off the curve. Refitted with this option: r = ${fmtR(v.r)}, ${v.sig ? "p < 0.05" : "p ≥ 0.05"} under ${DM.ruleLabel[v.rule]}.`
      : "Off the curve: the workshop holds no fitted analysis for this combination.";
    place(stageId);
    drawPanel();
  }

  const root = el("div", {class: "dm"}, legend, layout);
  update(null);
  const ro = new ResizeObserver(() => {
    const w = Math.floor(panel.clientWidth - 34);
    if (w > 0 && Math.abs(w - lastWidth) > 24) { place(latest === null ? null : (DM.stages.find(s => s.axes.includes(latest)) || {}).id); drawPanel(); }
  });
  ro.observe(root);
  const onMedia = () => { place(latest === null ? null : (DM.stages.find(s => s.axes.includes(latest)) || {}).id); drawPanel(); };
  wide.addEventListener("change", onMedia);
  invalidation.then(() => { ro.disconnect(); wide.removeEventListener("change", onMedia); });
  return root;
}
```

:::

The map uses the same three groups as the [menu](#level-estimand) below. The two measurement choices that also reach into the question – the rule for respondents who mention nothing and a published series covering only part of the panel – are marked in the estimand statement at the moment at which either choice is selected.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# This chunk follows the chunk of the decision map, which sorts curve by the
# claim-aligned r; it reads the curve again, in the order of the file, for the
# sections below.
axes <- c("outcome", "predictor", "copredictor", "estimator", "sample", "weights",
          "construction", "noop", "item_set", "cell_weight", "measure", "pred_form", "family")

curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
deviations <- readr::read_csv("data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
# every option swapped into the reproduced specification, read from the pairs file
ref_rows <- readr::read_csv("data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive") |>
  dplyr::semi_join(ref, by = axes)
bw <- readr::read_csv("data/display_between_within.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
inference <- readr::read_csv("data/display_inference.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
means <- readr::read_csv("data/display_country_means.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pw <- readr::read_csv("data/teney_panel_weights.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# fixed decimals and a true minus sign; percentages round halves up, as the
# decision map does, so that the map and the text print the same figures
num <- \(x, d = 3) sub("^-", "−", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(floor(x * 10^d + 0.5) / 10^d, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
pe <- \(p) if (p < 0.0001) "p < 0.0001" else paste("p =", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = if (p < 0.001) 4 else 3))

# shares of a set of curve rows below zero, and below zero with CR2 p < 0.05
below <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$r_ca < 0)
sig <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$r_ca < 0 & d$p_cr2 < 0.05)
sig_rule <- \(col) 100 * mean(curve$r_ca < 0 & curve[[col]] < 0.05)

# one value from the fork table, the option table or the reproduced specification;
# the filters inside these functions are those of dplyr, whose !! tells the
# arguments option and rule apart from the columns of the same names
fk <- \(axis, col = "share") forks[[col]][forks$axis == axis]
dv <- \(option, col, rule = NULL, which = "positive") {
  d <- dplyr::filter(deviations, curve == which, option == !!option)
  if (!is.null(rule)) d <- dplyr::filter(d, rule == !!rule)
  d[[col]][1]
}
rd <- \(option, col, rule = NULL) {
  d <- dplyr::filter(ref_rows, option == !!option)
  if (!is.null(rule)) d <- dplyr::filter(d, rule == !!rule)
  d[[col]][1]
}
bwv <- \(outcome, predictor, col) bw[[col]][bw$outcome == outcome & bw$predictor == predictor]
inf <- \(est, rule, col) inference[[col]][inference$estimator == est & inference$inference == rule]

# the questions fixed by the four decisions about the question that vary on the curve, and
# whether the measurement decisions and the form split each one across classes
questions <- curve |>
  datawizard::data_modify(cls = r_ca < 0 & p_cr2 < 0.05) |>
  dplyr::summarise(straddle = any(cls) & !all(cls),
                   .by = c(outcome, predictor, copredictor, estimator))
twoway <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, estimator == "fe_twoway")
country <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, estimator == "fe_country")
```

## The estimand statement

Write the statement that your analysis will complete:

> Among **which country-years**, with **each counting how much**, the association between **poor economic performance**, measured as **X**, and **positive EU framing**, measured as **Y**, comparing **what with what**, **holding what fixed**.

One question sorts the decisions: would two analysts who chose differently accept each other's number as an answer to the same question? If the two would not, the decision belongs to the question, and changing it rewrites a bold slot of the statement other than the two "measured as" slots. If they would, a decision about how a named construct becomes a column of numbers is a measurement decision and changes only a "measured as" slot, while any other decision belongs to the model and leaves the statement unchanged, given that the statement names what is estimated and says nothing about how the model is fitted or tested. The completed statement is your estimand [@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand], and a reader has to know it before any meaning can be attached to your coefficient.

Since the statement is written at the resolution of the claim, which names the constructs and the comparison but not the figures standing for them, the choice among published series of unemployment is a measurement decision. The scoring rule – whether a respondent's answers enter as a share of the respondent's own mentions or as a count of the items in the set – appears to be one as well, since both versions are built from the same thirteen items. The rule nevertheless belongs to the question, because a share and a count remain different quantities however well the items were measured, the one the weight of a framing among the frames held by a person and the other its volume. Two analysts who differ on the rule would thus not accept each other's number as an estimate of the same thing.

Two measurement decisions also reach into the question, and both are easily overlooked. Scoring respondents who mention nothing as zero retains every respondent in the cell mean, but the mean then equals the share among those who answered multiplied by the proportion who answered, the outcome thus mixing how people frame the EU with whether they name any meaning of it at all. A published series covering only part of the panel, in turn, is chosen as a measure of the predictor, yet it also changes the population of the question, since the country-years not covered by the series drop out of the analysis. The decision map marks both changes in the statement at the moment at which each is made.

The group to which a decision belongs also indicates the kind of reason required to justify it. A decision about the question requires an argument from the claim, since it determines the question itself, that is, the framing with which the claim is concerned, the measure of the economy, the comparison and the population. A measurement decision requires an argument from the instrument and the data, and a decision about the model an argument from the structure of the data, such as the bounds of a share or the correlation of a country with itself over time. An option off the curve may still be the right choice for a different question, and a reason of the right kind will usually indicate which question that is.

## The curve of 864 {#the-curve}

For each of the three positive scales scored as shares, the curve crosses the options that answer the claim: unemployment in four published series and in two forms, or GDP growth in the World Bank series; with or without the other economic measure held fixed; two-way or country fixed effects; respondents who mention nothing scored zero or left out; all 13 items or the 12 without "unemployment"; and cells as interviewed or weighted. These combinations yield 256 unemployment and 32 growth specifications for each scale, 288 per scale and 864 in all. Four decisions are fixed at a single option on the curve: all 270 country-years, no regression weight, the share as the scoring rule, and a linear model.

Each point on the curve is placed by its descriptive partial correlation, aligned with the claim so that values below zero lie in the direction predicted by the claim. The points are classed by errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which allow for the correlation of residuals within a country from year to year and for the few countries that carry most of the variation. Of the `r nrow(curve)` specifications, `r pct(below(curve))` lie below zero and `r pct(sig(curve))` lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, while the partial correlations range from `r num(min(curve$r_ca))` to `r num(max(curve$r_ca))`, with a median of `r num(median(curve$r_ca))`. The reproduced specification – the cosmopolitan share on World Bank unemployment under two-way fixed effects, with respondents who mention nothing scored zero – yields b = `r num(ref$b, 5)`, t = `r num(ref$t)` on `r ref$df` df and r = `r num(ref$r)`, the value targeted by the reproduction task, and its CR2 p-value of `r num(ref$p_cr2, 4)`, on `r num(ref$df_cr2, 1)` Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, lies just above the threshold of 5%.

Since almost every specification on the curve points in the direction of the claim, the uncertainty that remains appears to concern the strength of the evidence rather than its direction, and it is divided mainly by two decisions. Under country fixed effects `r pct(sig(country))` of the specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, compared with `r pct(sig(twoway))` under two-way fixed effects. With unemployment as the predictor the corresponding shares are `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(country, predictor == "unemp")))` and `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(twoway, predictor == "unemp")))`, while with growth they are `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, predictor == "growth")))` under both designs. @tbl-forks reports, for every decision that varies on the curve, the share of the variance carried by the decision and the frequency with which changing it alone alters the class of a specification.

| Decision | Group | Share of the variance | Class changes when moved alone |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Estimator | Question | `r pct(fk("estimator"))` | `r pct(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Predictor | Question | `r pct(fk("predictor"))` | `r pct(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Frame set | Question | `r pct(fk("outcome"))` | `r pct(fk("outcome", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Adjustment set | Question | `r pct(fk("copredictor"))` | `r pct(fk("copredictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Item set | Measurement | `r pct(fk("item_set"))` | `r pct(fk("item_set", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Respondents who mention nothing | Measurement | `r pct(fk("noop"))` | `r pct(fk("noop", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Published series | Measurement | `r pct(fk("measure"))` | `r pct(fk("measure", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Cell weighting | Measurement | `r pct(fk("cell_weight"))` | `r pct(fk("cell_weight", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Predictor form | Model | `r pct(fk("pred_form"))` | `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Interactions | – | `r pct(fk("interactions"))` | – |

: The decisions that vary on the curve of 864. The share of the variance is the share of the variance of the claim-aligned partial r that the decision carries as a main effect; the class changes are the share of pairs of specifications, differing only in that decision, whose members fall in different classes (below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, or not). The predictor pairs raw World Bank unemployment with World Bank growth. Source: `data/spec_curve_forks.csv`. {#tbl-forks}

The numbers on this page are computed from the files written to `data/` by the workshop's pipeline, namely the curve in `data/spec_curve.csv` and the comparison of every option with its twins on the curve in `data/menu_deviations.csv`, while `data/menu_options.csv` records for every option its status and the one-sentence reason printed by the helpers in the browser lab and in the workspace when the option is off the curve.

## The question {#level-estimand}

Each decision in this group rewrites the estimand statement, and two analysts who make it differently are therefore answering different questions.

| Decision | On the curve | Off the curve, and where it is taught | Share of the variance | Class changes |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| **Frame set** | cosmopolitan `mcosmo`, utilitarian `mutil`, positive composite `mpos` | communitarian `mcomm`, libertarian `mlib`, negative composite `mneg`, on a curve of their own | `r pct(fk("outcome"))` | `r pct(fk("outcome", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Scoring rule** | share of mentions `share` | count of items `count`, count per item `rate`, on [Scale construction](companion/measurement.qmd) | fixed | – |
| **Predictor** | unemployment `unemp`, GDP growth `growth` | – | `r pct(fk("predictor"))` | `r pct(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Adjustment set** | none `none`, the other measure `other` | – | `r pct(fk("copredictor"))` | `r pct(fk("copredictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Sample** | all 270 country-years `all` | 2004–2008 `y2004_2008`, 2009–2013 `y2009_2013`, without the bailout countries `no_bailout`, without Greece and Spain `no_GR_ES`, on [The multiverse and its critics](companion/multiverse.qmd) | fixed | – |
| **Whose average** | each country-year once `none` | respondents `n_cell`, effective sample size `n_eff`, adult population `pop`, in [Whose average](#whose-average) | fixed | – |
| **Estimator** | two-way fixed effects `fe_twoway`, country fixed effects `fe_country` | random effects `re`, pooled OLS `pooled_cl`, within–between model `rewb`, in [the module on panel data](companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-re) | `r pct(fk("estimator"))` | `r pct(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` |

: The seven decisions about the question. The last two columns describe the curve, as in @tbl-forks; "fixed" marks a decision with a single option on the curve. {#tbl-level1}

### Frame set

The original author groups the thirteen answer options offered by the question on what the EU means to the respondent into four dimensions, obtained by crossing the valence of a meaning with its content: cosmopolitan (positive and non-materialist), utilitarian (positive and materialist), communitarian (negative and non-materialist) and libertarian (negative and materialist), with a positive and a negative composite built from the two pairs. Since the claim names the positive dimensions, its outcomes are the cosmopolitan scale, the utilitarian scale and the positive composite. The composite arguably offers the plainest reading of "positive EU-framing dimensions", and the cosmopolitan scale is the one that the analysts were asked to use by the instruction for the second task in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The utilitarian scale, in turn, is the materialist dimension, on which the first hypothesis expects the stronger effect. On the curve the three scales give `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, outcome == "mcosmo")))`, `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, outcome == "mutil")))` and `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, outcome == "mpos")))` of specifications below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, and the frame set carries `r pct(fk("outcome"))` of the variance on the curve.

The three negative scales, which answer the other half of the first hypothesis, an increase in negative framing, have a curve of their own, `data/spec_curve_negative.csv`, aligned so that below zero is the direction of that half, but these scales do not constitute independent evidence for the claim. Under the share rule a respondent's four scales sum to one, and when respondents who mention nothing are scored zero, the positive and the negative composites of every country-year add up to one minus the share of respondents who mention nothing. Within countries the aligned negative composite and the positive composite correlate at 0.93, and a 'confirmation' on the negative composite thus largely counts the positive result a second time. The communitarian scale also contains the item "unemployment", which ties the outcome to the predictor by content, and removing that item reduces the aligned correlation of the scale at the reproduced specification from −0.495 to −0.290. The libertarian scale, finally, shows almost no association, and on the negative curve only `r pct(dv("mlib", "below_zero_sig", which = "negative"))` of its specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r pct(dv("mcomm", "below_zero_sig", which = "negative"))` for the communitarian scale and `r pct(dv("mneg", "below_zero_sig", which = "negative"))` for the negative composite. The relations among the thirteen items from which all of these scales are built are examined in [Scale construction](companion/measurement.qmd).

### Scoring rule

The scoring rule determines what "more" of a framing means. The share, which is the measure used in the paper, divides the items of a scale that a respondent mentions by all the items that the respondent mentions, which makes it a relative frequency, since whatever else a respondent mentions lowers the share of every scale. The count, by contrast, is the number of items in the scale that a respondent mentions, regardless of anything else that the respondent mentions, and the rate divides the count by the number of items in the scale, placing a two-item and a five-item scale on one footing. Since the claim concerns how citizens frame the EU, which is arguably a matter of composition, the share is the only rule on the curve.

The count measures something else, namely the volume of what people say about the EU. Across the country-years the cosmopolitan count correlates `r num(cor(pw$c_mcosmo, pw$mean_items), 2)` with the mean number of items mentioned by respondents, compared with `r num(cor(pw$w_mcosmo, pw$mean_items), 2)` for the share, and the two constructions of the cosmopolitan outcome correlate at only `r num(cor(pw$w_mcosmo, pw$c_mcosmo), 2)`. A count therefore appears to answer a neighbouring question, whether people say more or fewer positive things about the EU, and since it is the construct used by KEVF1 and 018OL, the difference matters for the interpretation of the results reported by these two analysts. Swapped into the specifications of the curve, the count leaves `r pct(dv("count", "below_zero_sig"))` of them below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r pct(sig(curve))` on the curve, and at the reproduced specification it shifts the aligned correlation from `r num(ref$r_ca)` to `r num(rd("count", "r_ca_dev"))` (CR2 `r pe(rd("count", "p_dev"))`). In a linear model the rate yields exactly the same test and partial correlation as the count, since it divides the count by a constant, and it serves as the form of the count that a beta regression can take.

### Predictor

The claim names "poor economic performances", of which the paper models two measures, the national unemployment rate and annual GDP growth, both of which are justifiable readings and remain on the curve. Unemployment is also the measure named in the instruction for the second task in the robustness study. Growth, however, contains less information within countries, since 59% of its within-country variation is common to all countries in the same year – in particular the recession of 2009 – and is removed by the year effects of the two-way design. The within-country slope of growth on the cosmopolitan scale is small (`r num(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "b_within"), 5)`, CR2 `r pe(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "p_within_cr2"))`), whereas across the 27 country means the association is clear (`r num(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "b_between"), 4)`, `r pe(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "p_between"))`). Since the claim expects framing to rise with growth, the sign of every growth specification is reversed on the curve. Switching from unemployment to growth, with everything else held fixed, changes the class of `r pct(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs, and growth specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 in `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, predictor == "growth")))` of cases, against `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, predictor == "unemp")))` for unemployment.

### Adjustment set

With unemployment as the predictor, leaving growth out yields the association of framing with unemployment regardless of what happened to output, while holding growth fixed yields the association at a given rate of growth, the roles being reversed when growth is the predictor. The two options may thus be regarded as two estimands rather than as a right and a wrong set of controls, which is why both remain on the curve. The unadjusted slope is the one estimated by the reproduced specification, whereas the adjusted slope follows the original study, whose model includes both measures. Under the principle that the controls defining an estimand belong in every model of it [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational], the two slopes are better kept as two estimands, each with its own definition, than mixed as interchangeable variants of one. Whether growth is a common cause, a second expression of the downturn or a step on the path from the crisis to framing is a question addressed by the [causal graph](companion/dags.qmd). On the curve the decision carries `r pct(fk("copredictor"))` of the variance and changes the class of `r pct(fk("copredictor", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs.

### Sample

The population of the claim comprises the 27 member states over 2004–2013, that is, the 270 country-years of the panel, and this population is the only sample on the curve. Each of the four restrictions on the menu answers a question about a different population, which is why the sample counts as a decision about the question, and none of the restrictions offers a second way of answering the claim as written. The restrictions are conventionally treated as robustness checks, but a check that changes the population also changes the estimand statement, and its result can therefore neither confirm nor undermine an answer about another population.

- **2004–2008** retains only the years before the crisis reached most labour markets. A window containing no crisis cannot speak to whether the crisis undermined positive framing, and within countries it measures how framing tracked the smaller fluctuations of those years.
- **2009–2013** retains only the crisis years, thereby dropping the comparison with the preceding period and asking how framing moved with the deepening and easing of the crisis once it had begun.
- **Without the bailout countries** removes the eight countries that received financial assistance (Cyprus, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Portugal, Romania and Spain), in which the crisis was deepest and which carry most of the variation in unemployment that identifies the slope. The question then becomes whether the association holds in the countries in which the crisis was mild.
- **Without Greece and Spain** is an influence diagnostic, a check on how much the result owes to the two countries with the largest rises in unemployment, of the kind listed by @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed among the forms of nonequivalence as unstable country subsets. A single hand-picked exclusion is arguably a weak form of the diagnostic, which is performed more completely by leaving out one country at a time.

Splitting the panel at 2008 is one rung of a ladder of ways to handle the crisis years, ranging from pooling the crisis years with the other years, as in the full panel, through a crisis indicator or a split into periods, to absorbing every year with its own effect, as in the two-way design.

Swapped into the specifications of the curve, the four restrictions leave `r pct(dv("y2004_2008", "below_zero_sig"))` (2004–2008), `r pct(dv("y2009_2013", "below_zero_sig"))` (2009–2013), `r pct(dv("no_bailout", "below_zero_sig"))` (without the bailout countries) and `r pct(dv("no_GR_ES", "below_zero_sig"))` (without Greece and Spain) below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r pct(sig(curve))` on the curve, and the sign changes in `r pct(dv("no_bailout", "sign_changes"))` of the pairs without the bailout countries. The findings yielded by the restrictions are presented instead in three displays in [The multiverse and its critics](companion/multiverse.qmd#sec-heterogeneity) – the slope by period, the slope with one country left out at a time, and the bailout countries against the rest – leaving the curve with a single population.

### Whose average

Unweighted, every country-year counts once and the slope describes the average member state – with Malta counting as much as Germany – which matches a claim about how the economy of a country shapes the ways in which its citizens frame the EU. Weighting by the number of respondents in a country-year (`n_cell`), or by their effective number discounted for the unevenness of the survey weights (`n_eff`), rests on an argument from precision, since if the cell means differed only in how precisely they are measured, weighting by sample size would estimate the same quantity more efficiently. Weighting by adult population (`pop`) changes the quantity to the average European, for whom the largest member state counts `r num(max(pw$pop_15plus) / min(pw$pop_15plus), 0)` times as much as the smallest.

Only the unweighted fit remains on the curve, because the argument from precision does not hold on these data, in which sampling error makes up a small part of the variation between country-years, about 7% of what the reproduced model leaves unexplained. Efficient weights are therefore close to equal, and the respondent weights mostly shift weight towards the years with two survey waves and towards the countries with the largest samples, while the population weight answers a defensible but different question, one that the claim does not ask. Swapped into the specifications of the curve, the respondent weight leaves `r pct(dv("n_cell", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 and the effective sample size `r pct(dv("n_eff", "below_zero_sig"))`, while the population weight leaves `r pct(dv("pop", "below_zero_sig"))` and changes the class of `r pct(dv("pop", "class_changes"))` of the pairs.

### Estimator

The estimator determines which country-years are compared with which, and of all the decisions on the curve it moves the results most, with `r pct(fk("estimator"))` of the variance, while two fixed-effects designs remain on the curve as two estimands. Two-way fixed effects removes the stable differences between countries and whatever all member states went through together in a year, the slope thus comparing each country with itself relative to the common European path. Country fixed effects, by contrast, retains the changes common to Europe in a given year, which on this panel make up 29% of the within-country variation in unemployment, and its comparison therefore includes the common path. Its slope is larger, and the design is exposed to confounding by any shift in framing across Europe that coincided with the crisis. At the reproduced specification the two designs yield r = `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "r_descriptive"))` (CR2 p = `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)`) and r = `r num(inf("fe_country", "conventional", "r_descriptive"))` (CR2 `r pe(inf("fe_country", "cr2_satterthwaite", "p"))`), and across the curve switching between the two changes the class of `r pct(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs. Year effects, which absorb every year with its own effect, form the last rung of the ladder described in the section on the sample.

**Pooled OLS** regresses framing on unemployment across all 270 country-years at once, and its slope thus mixes the stable differences between countries with the changes within countries, two associations that run in opposite directions on these data, as shown in [the module on panel data](companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-pooled). A pooled slope therefore answers neither the within-country reading of the claim nor the cross-national one. Swapped into the specifications of the curve, pooled OLS leaves `r pct(dv("pooled_cl", "below_zero"))` of them below zero and `r pct(dv("pooled_cl", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, and the sign changes in `r pct(dv("pooled_cl", "sign_changes"))` of the pairs, a pattern that appears more consistent with a different quantity than with a noisy version of the same one.

**Random effects** fits a single slope that is a weighted blend of the within-country and the between-country associations, and the estimator is consistent only if the stable differences between countries are unrelated to the predictor. This assumption does not hold on the country-year panel, where the within and the between slopes have opposite signs in `r sum(sign(bw$b_within) != sign(bw$b_between))` of the `r nrow(bw)` combinations of positive scale and predictor. The test of the difference between the two slopes rejects at the 5% level in `r sum(bw$p_difference < 0.05)` of those combinations, as described in [the module on panel data](companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-random-effects). Swapped into the specifications of the curve, the estimator leaves `r pct(dv("re", "below_zero_sig", "re_cr1_g1"))` below zero with p < 0.05 under errors clustered by country, a figure that probably owes as much to the comparison made by the estimator as to the evidence.

**The within–between model** of @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects separates what random effects blend, with the deviation of the predictor from its country mean carrying the within slope and the country mean carrying the between slope. Since its within slope equals the fixed-effects slope exactly, the model would repeat points already on the curve with other errors, and its place is therefore in [the module on panel data](companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-within-between). There the model presents the two associations side by side, and for the cosmopolitan scale the test of the difference between them gives `r pe(bwv("mcosmo", "unemp", "p_difference"))`.

## Measurement {#level-measurement}

With the question held fixed, the decisions in this group change how a named construct becomes a column of numbers.

| Decision | On the curve | Off the curve, and where it is taught | Share of the variance | Class changes |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| **Respondents who mention nothing** | scored zero `zero`, left out `drop` | split rule `split`; multiple imputation `mi_mice`, `mi_amelia`, on [Scale construction](companion/measurement.qmd#sec-noop) | `r pct(fk("noop"))` | `r pct(fk("noop", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Item set** | all 13 items `all`, without "unemployment" `un` | – | `r pct(fk("item_set"))` | `r pct(fk("item_set", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Cell weighting** | as interviewed `unweighted`, weighted `design` | – | `r pct(fk("cell_weight"))` | `r pct(fk("cell_weight", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Published series** | unemployment: World Bank `wb_nat`, Eurostat 15–74 `es_1574_act`, Eurostat 20–64 as a share of the population `es_2064_pop`, Labour Force Survey 25–64 `es_2564_lfs`; growth: World Bank `wb_growth` | Eurostat table tipsun20 `es_1574_tips`, Eurostat growth `es_growth`, on [Social science data sources](companion/data-sources.qmd) | `r pct(fk("measure"))` | `r pct(fk("measure", "crossing_rate"))` |

: The four measurement decisions, with the last two columns as in @tbl-forks. {#tbl-level2}

### Respondents who mention nothing

Of all respondents, `r pct(100 * sum(pw$n_noop) / sum(pw$n_cy))` mention none of the 13 items, and since these respondents have no share at all under the share rule, a decision has to be made about them. Scoring them zero, the rule adopted in the country-year panel and in the reproduced specification, retains every respondent but changes the construct, since the cell mean then equals the share among those who answered multiplied by the proportion who answered, which lets the rate of saying nothing enter every scale. Leaving these respondents out is consistent with the share as a measure, given that a respondent with no mentions has no share, and corresponds to the procedure followed in the code of the original study, although it comes at the cost of conditioning on answering. Since the rate of saying nothing falls slightly within countries as unemployment rises (b = −0.0011 per point; t = −1.25 with errors clustered by country), the zero rule pulls the slopes a little towards zero. Both rules remain on the curve, where the drop rule gives `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, noop == "drop")))` of specifications below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 and the zero rule `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, noop == "zero")))`.

The split rule, which leaves out those who said "don't know" or gave no answer and scores off-list answers as zero, yields a construct arguably no clearer than that of either rule on the curve, and its results lie close to those of the two rules (`r pct(dv("split", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05). The two imputation rules fill in the shares of the silent respondents under a missing-at-random assumption, but since the imputations were computed only at the standard measurement settings, the two rules cannot be crossed with the rest of the menu. What each rule assumes about the people who stayed silent is described in the section [Respondents who mention nothing](companion/measurement.qmd#sec-noop) of the module on scale construction.

### Item set

The original author builds every scale from the 13 items used in the paper, while the code of the original study also builds a second version without the item "unemployment", in which the communitarian scale and every denominator are one item shorter. When more people name "unemployment" as a meaning of the EU, every other share falls mechanically, and part of a decline in positive shares may thus reflect the rise of that one item rather than a change in how positively the EU is framed. Both sets remain on the curve, and the shift between them corresponds to the part of the result attributable to the overlap. With all items `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, item_set == "all")))` of specifications lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, and without "unemployment" `r pct(sig(datawizard::data_filter(curve, item_set == "un")))`. Under the reduced set a respondent whose only mention was "unemployment" is left with nothing and joins the respondents who mention nothing.

### Cell weighting

The cell mean can be the mean of the respondents as interviewed, as in the original study and the country-year panel, or the mean under the post-stratification weight supplied by GESIS, an estimate of the mean of the national population. The weighted mean is in principle the better estimator of a national quantity, but the design effects are small, and the decision explains `r pct(fk("cell_weight"), 2)` of the variance on the curve and changes the class of `r pct(fk("cell_weight", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs. Both options remain on the curve, although if a leaner menu were wanted, this would arguably be the first decision to fix.

### Published series

The five analysts merged five different unemployment series, differing in age band and denominator. The four series that cover all 270 country-years move together within countries, correlating between 0.995 and 0.999 once country and year means are removed, and all four remain on the curve, where the decision explains `r pct(fk("measure"))` of the variance. The Eurostat table tipsun20, merged by KEVF1, is a different matter, since it has no row for the United Kingdom and, before 2009, rows only for France and Sweden, and choosing it therefore leaves `r rd("es_1574_tips", "n_cells_dev")` of the 270 country-years. Such a choice is arguably a decision about the sample presented as a decision about the measure, and its results describe another population and another period. Swapped into the unemployment specifications of the curve, the table leaves `r pct(dv("es_1574_tips", "below_zero_sig"))` of them below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, a figure that probably reflects the crisis years, which make up most of its cells, more than the series itself. Since the Eurostat growth series has no row for the United Kingdom either, choosing it removes a country from the population, and only the World Bank growth series remains on the curve.

## The model {#level-estimation}

With the question and the measures held fixed, the decisions in this group change the model that is fitted and how certain its answer is said to be. Two of the three concern the fit and can move the estimate, whereas the third concerns the inference and moves only the class.

| Decision | On the curve | Off the curve, and where it is taught | Share of the variance | Class changes |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| **Predictor form** | raw `raw`, logged `log` (unemployment only) | – | `r pct(fk("pred_form"), 2)` | `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Outcome family** | linear `gaussian` | beta regression `beta`, in [Outcome family](#outcome-family) | fixed | – |
| **Inference** | CR2 with Satterthwaite df `cr2` | clustered, CR1 `cr1`, conventional `conventional`, in [the module on panel data](companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-inference) | nil | – |

: The three decisions about the model: two about the fit, one about the inference. The inference cannot change the partial correlation, so its share of the variance is nil. {#tbl-level3}

### Predictor form

Unemployment enters either raw, in which case each percentage point counts the same, or logged, in which case each proportional rise counts the same, a rise from 4% to 8% counting as much as one from 10% to 20%. Both forms are defensible statements of how a crisis might act on framing, and since the claim does not choose between them, both remain on the curve. Growth enters raw only, given that it takes negative values, while centring and standardising do not constitute separate analyses, because shifting or rescaling the predictor cannot move t, r or p. The form explains almost none of the variance on the curve (`r pct(fk("pred_form"), 2)`), yet changing it alone alters the class of `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs.

### Outcome family

Whereas the linear model fits the cell means directly, the beta family fits them through a logit link with a likelihood that respects the bounds of a share. Both models describe the same conditional mean, and neither offers a different answer to the claim. The bounds matter for the utilitarian scale, whose cell means come close to zero, while the cosmopolitan and positive cell means lie well inside the unit interval. The beta family barely moves the results, leaving `r pct(dv("beta", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with p < 0.05 under errors clustered by country when swapped into the specifications of the curve, with a median shift in the aligned correlation of `r num(dv("beta", "median_shift"))`. The family remains off the curve because clubSandwich, which computes the CR2 rule by which the curve is classed, does not cover beta regression, and including the family would thus put two inference rules on one curve. It serves instead as a check of the functional form, available for the share and the rate but not for the count, which is not a proportion.

### Inference

The inference rules all estimate the same slope, differing only in the uncertainty that they attach to it. Conventional errors treat the 270 country-years as independent, which they are not, since in the reproduced model the residuals within a country correlate 0.53 from one year to the next.
