The standard clustered errors (CR1, tested on 26 df) allow for that correlation but overstate the evidence when a few of the 27 countries carry most of the variation that identifies the slope, as is the case here. The curve is therefore classed by the CR2 correction of @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard, tested on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom in the form of @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust, a correction that adjusts the clustered errors for the unequal influence of the countries. The degrees of freedom, whose median on the curve is `r num(stats::median(curve$df_cr2), 1)`, indicate how many countries effectively carry the information, and the three rules are described in [the module on panel data](companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-inference).

@tbl-inference reports the reproduced specification under each rule. While the partial correlation remains the same throughout, the p-value ranges from `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "p"), 5)` under conventional errors to `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)` under CR2, which is why the workshop does not call the reproduced result significant at 5% without stating under which errors. Across the curve, the share of specifications below zero with p < 0.05 is `r pct(sig_rule("p_conv"))` under conventional errors, `r pct(sig_rule("p_cr1"))` under CR1 and `r pct(sig_rule("p_cr2"))` under CR2.

| Rule | t | df | p | r from the conversion formula |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Conventional | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "t"))` | `r inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "df")` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "p"), 5)` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "r_formula"))` |
| Clustered by country, CR1 | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "t"))` | `r inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "df")` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "p"))` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "r_formula"))` |
| CR2, Satterthwaite df | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "t"))` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "df"), 1)` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "r_formula"))` |

: One estimate under three kinds of inference: the reproduced specification, b = `r num(ref$b, 5)`, whose descriptive partial correlation is `r num(ref$r)` under every rule. Source: `data/display_inference.csv`. {#tbl-inference}

The last column illustrates why the curve plots the descriptive partial correlation and tests it separately, since the conversion r = t / sqrt(t^2^ + df) recovers the partial correlation only from the conventional t and the residual df, and when fed a clustered t with its smaller df returns a larger number although the evidence is weaker, a trap described on [the background page](background.qmd#sec-conversion).

## Admissible combinations {#admissibility}

Not every combination of options exists, and the browser lab and the workspace warn you when you have combined two options that do not go together:

- **Published series ← predictor.** The unemployment series go with unemployment and the growth series with growth.
- **Predictor form ← predictor.** GDP growth takes negative values and enters raw only.
- **Imputed answers ← the standard settings.** The two imputation engines were run with raw unemployment in the World Bank series, all items and cells as interviewed, and they therefore combine only with those settings.
- **Outcome family ← scoring rule.** The beta family requires a proportion strictly between 0 and 1, which the share and the rate provide and the count does not.
- **Off-curve options ← one at a time.** Each option off the curve was fitted against the specifications of the curve with every other decision on its curve options, and a combination of two off-curve options, such as a count under pooled OLS, was therefore never fitted.

---

## Claim alignment {#the-claim-alignment-step}

Every outcome on the curve is a positive framing, for which the claim predicts a **negative** coefficient on unemployment, and for unemployment specifications the partial correlation therefore needs no alignment, since below zero already is the direction of the claim. A single flip remains for the growth specifications, since when the predictor is GDP growth the claim predicts a **positive** coefficient on the positive framings, and the claim-aligned value therefore multiplies b, t and r by −1 (the lab applies this for you). After the flip, below zero means the direction of the claim for every specification on the curve, whatever it measures.

The negative scales have a curve of their own, on which the alignment is reversed so that below zero is the direction of the other half of the first hypothesis, an increase in negative framing. Reversing the sign of r there is equivalent to reverse-coding the negative scale as 1 − y before fitting, which flips the sign of the coefficient and leaves its standard error, |t| and p-value untouched, alignment thus changing the direction in which the evidence is stated but nothing about the evidence itself.

---

## Worked example

**Choice:** frame set `mpos`, scoring rule `share`, predictor `unemp`, adjustment `none`, sample `all`, whose average `none`, estimator `fe_twoway`; respondents who mention nothing `drop`, item set `all`, cell weighting `unweighted`, series `wb_nat`; form `raw`, family `gaussian`, inference by CR2 errors clustered by country with Satterthwaite df.

**Justification, by group.** The claim speaks of positive dimensions in the plural, which the composite scale captures more directly than the cosmopolitan scale alone, and the share is kept because the claim concerns how people frame the EU rather than how much they say about it. The comparison that the claim makes is that of a country with itself as its economy deteriorates, net of whatever all member states went through together in a year, which is what two-way fixed effects estimate; nothing in the claim restricts the countries or the years, and the claim is about countries, so every country-year counts once. Respondents who mention nothing are left out, following the code of the original study, because a person with no framing of the EU is not a person with zero positive framing, and the World Bank series is kept because it is the series on which the panel was built. The raw percentage is kept because the claim gives no warrant for a proportional effect, and the slope is tested with CR2 errors clustered by country and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, because the residuals of a country correlate from year to year and a few countries carry most of the variation.

A justification of this kind renders a specification defensible, since it connects each choice either to the wording of the claim or to an argument about the data, according to the group to which the choice belongs.

---

## Justifying each decision {#what-each-decision-commits-you-to}

A decision may explain almost none of the variance on the curve and still determine whether *your* result clears p = 0.05, because significance is a property of a single specification and variance a property of the whole set. The rule for respondents who mention nothing explains `r pct(fk("noop"))` of the variance and changes the class of `r pct(fk("noop", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs, while the predictor form explains `r pct(fk("pred_form"), 2)` and changes `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))`. If the question is fixed by fixing the four decisions about it that vary on the curve, while the measurement decisions and the form are left free, `r sum(questions$straddle)` of the `r nrow(questions)` questions still contain both a specification below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 and one that is not, which is why you fix your specification in the preregistration before you run it.
